questions.q: The debugger is paused on const subtotal = cartSubtotal(lines);. You want to see the first line inside cartSubtotal. Which command?
questions.explain: Step into enters the function called on the current line. Step over would run the whole call and stop on the next line of checkoutTotal.

questions.q: You stepped into a helper by mistake and are now on its first line. What does step out do?
questions.explain: Step out finishes the current function (it still runs; nothing is skipped) and pauses in the caller. Debuggers cannot go backwards.
options: Leaves the debugger and lets the program finish
Goes back to the previous line
Runs the rest of the helper and pauses right after it returns to the caller
Skips the helper without running it

questions.q: What does a debugger; statement do when the program runs normally, with no debugger attached?
questions.explain: debugger is a breakpoint written in code. Without an attached debugger it is ignored. With DevTools open, it pauses, which is why you should never commit one.

questions.q: A loop processes 20,000 orders and order 7431 comes out wrong. What is the best breakpoint?
questions.explain: A conditional breakpoint only pauses when its expression is true, so the program runs at full speed until the one iteration you care about.
options: A normal breakpoint in the loop, then press continue 7,430 times
A conditional breakpoint in the loop with the condition order.id === 7431
A breakpoint on the first line of the file

questions.q: A payment request times out after 5 seconds. Pausing at a breakpoint inside it makes it time out every time. What should you use to see the values?
questions.explain: Pausing freezes the program, and timers keep counting in the other system. A logpoint behaves like a console.log added without editing the code, so the timing stays realistic.
options: A logpoint: it prints the values without pausing
Step over instead of step into

questions.q: What is a watch expression?
questions.explain: Watches save you from typing the same exec at every pause. They can be any expression: typeof delivery, cart.length, total > 10_000_000.
options: An expression that stops the program when its value changes
An expression the debugger re-evaluates and shows every time the program pauses
A variable that is logged to a file
A breakpoint that watches the network

questions.q: What is the difference between breakOnException and breakOnUncaught in node inspect?
questions.explain: Pausing on every exception is noisy in code that throws and catches on purpose; pausing on uncaught ones only shows the crashes. Both leave you paused with the variables alive.
options: breakOnException only works in the browser
breakOnException pauses on every thrown error, even one that is caught later; breakOnUncaught only on errors nobody catches
breakOnUncaught pauses before the error is created

questions.q: A script crashes within 50 milliseconds of starting, before you can attach Chrome DevTools. Which flag helps?
questions.explain: --inspect-brk pauses before the first line until a debugger attaches. --inspect would let the script run (and crash) straight away.

questions.q: Why must a production server never run with --inspect=0.0.0.0:9229?
questions.explain: The inspector protocol can evaluate any expression in your process: read secrets, change data, spawn programs. It listens on 127.0.0.1 by default; keep it that way, and reach a remote server through an SSH tunnel.
options: Anyone who can reach the port can run arbitrary code inside the process

questions.q: A staging server runs node --inspect app.js (listening on 127.0.0.1). How do you debug it from your laptop safely?
questions.explain: The SSH tunnel makes the remote port appear on your own machine without exposing it to the network. The inspector still only accepts local connections on the server.
options: Change it to listen on 0.0.0.0 for a few minutes
Forward the port over SSH (ssh -L 9229:localhost:9229 server) and attach to localhost:9229
Copy the server's memory to your laptop

questions.q: In a VS Code launch configuration, what does "skipFiles": ["<node_internals>/**"] do?
questions.explain: Skipped files still run; the debugger just steps through them as if they were one line. Adding node_modules/** does the same for libraries.
options: Stops those files from being loaded
Makes stepping skip Node.js's own internal code, so step into never lands in node:internal
Hides those files from the stack trace in logs

questions.q: What is the quickest way to debug npm run dev in VS Code without writing a launch configuration?
questions.explain: The JavaScript Debug Terminal attaches VS Code's debugger to Node.js processes it starts, including those started through npm scripts, tsx or test runners.
options: Run it in a JavaScript Debug Terminal; every Node.js process started there is attached automatically

questions.q: console.log(order) prints address: { city: 'Lagos', geo: [Object] }. How do you see what is inside geo?
questions.explain: Node's console.log stops at depth 2 and abbreviates deeper objects as [Object]. depth: null means "no limit".
options: You cannot; [Object] means it is empty

questions.q: Why give an Account class a [util.inspect.custom]() method that hides apiToken?
questions.explain: The custom inspect method controls how Node.js prints the object. It does not affect JSON.stringify (use toJSON for that) or a debugger, which runs on your machine and may see real values.
options: So that the debugger cannot see the token
So that every console.log or util.inspect of an account, including future debug logs, leaves the token out

questions.q: An object has a private field #pin. Where can you see its value while debugging?
questions.explain: console.log in Node.js does not print private fields, and JSON ignores them. The debugger shows the real object, private fields included.
options: In the debugger's Scope section when paused
Nowhere; private fields cannot be inspected at all

questions.q: Clicking "Pay" on a page does something unexpected, and you do not know which of 40 scripts handles the click. What is the fastest way in?
questions.explain: An event listener breakpoint pauses in whatever code runs for that event, so the debugger finds the handler for you.
options: Sources → Event Listener Breakpoints → Mouse → click, then click the button

questions.q: An element's class keeps being reset by some script. Which breakpoint finds the script?
questions.explain: DOM change breakpoints pause at the line of JavaScript that changes the element, with the full call stack of who asked for the change.
options: Elements → right-click the element → Break on → attribute modifications

questions.q: await res.json() throws SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<', "<!doctype "... is not valid JSON. What is the most likely situation?
questions.explain: JSON never starts with <; HTML does. Look at the status and content type in the Network panel: the request probably went to a wrong URL or failed on the server.
options: The JSON has a trailing comma
The server sent an HTML page (often an error page, like a 404) instead of JSON
JSON cannot contain the letter d

questions.q: A request "doesn't work". In which order should you look at the response?
questions.explain: The status says whether it worked at all, the content type says what kind of body to expect, and only then does the body make sense. Many parsing errors are really wrong statuses.
options: Status, then content type, then body

questions.q: A login form submits, the page redirects, and the failing request disappears from the Network panel. What do you turn on?
questions.explain: By default the Network panel clears on navigation. Preserve log keeps requests across reloads and redirects.

questions.q: Why is "Copy as cURL" useful when debugging a browser request?
questions.explain: With the exact request in a command, you can test the server without the page, vary one header at a time, and attach it to a bug report.
options: It gives you a command that repeats the exact request (URL, headers, body) from a terminal: a reproduction anyone can run
It converts the response to JSON

questions.q: What does node --enable-source-maps dist/main.js change?
questions.explain: The map records which output position came from which source position. Node uses it to rewrite each frame of a stack trace.
options: It recompiles the TypeScript before running
Stack traces name the original .ts files and lines, using the .js.map files
It type-checks the code at runtime
It makes the program run faster

questions.q: Why does the mappings string in a source map store differences between positions instead of the positions themselves?
questions.explain: Neighbouring positions are close together, so their differences are tiny, and VLQ writes small numbers in one character. Absolute line and column numbers would make the map several times larger.
options: Differences are small numbers, which need fewer base64 VLQ characters, so the map stays small
Because browsers require it for security
So that the map works for any source file

questions.q: A stack trace from your server points at a line of TypeScript that is a blank line. What should you suspect first?
questions.explain: A map only makes sense for the exact output it was generated with. If one was rebuilt and the other not, every position is translated wrongly.
options: The .js and .js.map files are from different builds; rebuild both
The error was thrown by a comment
Source maps do not work with ES modules

questions.q: What happens when a public website serves its .map files?
questions.explain: Source maps usually contain (or point to) the original sources. That is fine for open source; otherwise upload maps privately to your error tracker and do not serve them.
options: Anyone can read the original, unminified source, including comments
The site becomes slower for all users
Users' browsers refuse to run the code

questions.q: Why do stack traces from node app.ts (Node's type stripping) point at the right .ts lines without any source map?
questions.explain: Stripping keeps the positions: erased types become whitespace. Transforming compilers (tsc, bundlers) move code around, which is why they need maps.
options: Node compiles TypeScript with tsc internally
Type stripping replaces type annotations with spaces, so every line and column stays where it was
Node ignores line numbers for TypeScript
Node downloads the map from npm

questions.q: Checkout failed for 12 customers last night between 01:00 and 01:20, and it works now. Which tool helps most?
questions.explain: You cannot pause the past. Debuggers observe a program running now; for a problem that already happened, only what was logged at the time can tell you what happened.
options: A breakpoint in the checkout handler
The structured logs from that time window
The Network panel in your browser

questions.q: The settings came from environment variables. What does this print?
questions.explain: + with a string joins text. - has no string meaning, so it converts both sides to numbers and subtracts. That is why the bug only shows where amounts are added.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With a number on one side, the string is converted and compared numerically. With strings on both sides, they are compared character by character: "9" comes after "5", so "900" >= "5000000" is true.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Query strings, form fields and environment variables only carry text. "true" is a non-empty string, not the boolean true. Convert settings once, when they are loaded.
questions.code:
const settings = Object.fromEntries(new URLSearchParams("feeKobo=150000&freeDelivery=true"));
console.log(typeof settings.feeKobo, typeof settings.freeDelivery, settings.freeDelivery === true);

questions.q: This uses EventTarget, the same listener machinery as DOM elements. The page re-renders after every click. What does it print?
questions.explain: Every render adds another listener, and each click runs all of them. Click 1 runs 1 listener (1 item), click 2 runs 2 (3 items), click 3 runs 3 (6 items). A count that grows faster with each action is the classic symptom of listeners registered in code that runs repeatedly.

questions.q: What does this print when run normally?
questions.explain: With no debugger attached, debugger does nothing, and the function returns the sum.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: res.ok is true for statuses 200 to 299 only. A 204 is a success with no body, so it is ok but must not be parsed as JSON.

questions.q: What does this print in Node.js?
questions.explain: The request succeeded; there is simply nothing to parse. An empty body is not valid JSON. Check for 204 (or an empty body) before calling json().
options:
true 204
SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input

false 204
SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input

questions.q: This is the base64 VLQ decoder from the lesson. What does it print?
questions.explain: O is digit 14; the lowest bit is the sign (0, positive), so the value is 14 >> 1 = 7: "source line +7", which is why JavaScript line 1 maps to TypeScript line 8. C is 2 → +1, and D is 3 → odd, so −1.

questions.q: What does this print in Node.js?
questions.explain: console.log shows nested objects down to depth 2 (the top level is depth 0). features is at depth 3, so it is abbreviated. Use console.dir(booking, { depth: null }) to see it.
questions.code:
const booking = { id: 7, guest: { name: "Ada", room: { floor: 2, features: { balcony: true } } } };
console.log(booking);
options: { id: 7, guest: { name: 'Ada', room: { floor: 2, features: { balcony: true } } } }

questions.q: What does this print in Node.js?
questions.explain: The custom inspect method changes what console.log prints, but JSON.stringify ignores it and still leaks the full card number. For JSON logs, add a toJSON() method with the same redaction.
options:
Customer(Chidi, card ending 1234)
Customer(Chidi, card ending 1234)

questions.q: Write loadSettings(query) that reads a query string with URLSearchParams and returns an object whose values are whole numbers. Throw an Error naming the setting when a value is not a non-negative integer.
questions.explain: Converting once at load time means no other code can receive a string by accident. "15OO" (letter O instead of zero) becomes NaN, which is not an integer, so it is refused with a message that names the setting.
questions.expected:
1915000
Setting deliveryFeeKobo must be whole kobo, got "15OO"

questions.q: Write readJson(res): throw Error("Request failed: STATUS") when the response is not ok, return null for status 204, and otherwise return the parsed JSON.
questions.explain: Checking the status first turns a confusing "Unexpected token '<'" into a clear "Request failed: 404", and handles the empty 204 body instead of trying to parse it.

questions.q: Fix the listener pile-up: rewrite the code so that render only updates what is shown, and the click listener is registered exactly once, at setup. Three clicks must print 1, 2, 3.
questions.explain: Code that runs repeatedly (render functions, loops, request handlers) must not register listeners or timers. Register once, at setup, and let the listener call render.

questions.q: A conditional breakpoint with order.discountKobo > order.totalKobo would pause at the first bad order. Write firstBadOrder(orders) that returns the id of that order, or null if there is none, so you know which iteration to expect.
questions.explain: find stops at the first match, exactly like a conditional breakpoint pauses at the first iteration where its condition is true. Order 103 is also bad, but you only reach it after continuing.

questions.q: Imitate a logpoint: finish cartSubtotal so that, after each line is added, it prints SKU subtotal=N. It must still return the subtotal.
questions.explain: A logpoint prints a message with values at a line every time it runs, without pausing. In an editor you add it by right-clicking the line number, and it disappears when you remove it, with no code change to forget.

questions.q: Write redact(object, keys) that returns a copy of the object where the listed keys are replaced by "[redacted]", for safe logging. The original must not change.
questions.explain: Spreading into a new object copies the top level, so the real account keeps its values. Redacting by key name is how most loggers keep tokens and passwords out of log files.

questions.q: Write describeResponse(res) that returns "STATUS CONTENT-TYPE: first 20 characters of the body", the three things to check for any failed request, in that order.
questions.explain: Reading the body as text never throws, unlike json(), so this works for any response. Status, content type and the start of the body tell you almost every time whether the problem is the request, the server or your parsing.
